title: VISp history did not improve prediction between two movie clips in eight mouse recordings
abstract: We tested whether a fixed neural read-out transfers between two Allen natural-movie clips and whether VISp history improves transfer. We used 1,051 quality-filtered cortical units from the first eight Visual Coding sessions by session ID. Each draw used four predictor mice, four target mice, 100 predictor units and 25 target units per area. Models were fitted and tuned only on the training clip. Current VISp explained mean higher-area signal shares of 0.149 and 0.071 in the two transfer directions. One second of independent VISp lag coefficients changed prediction by -3.46 percentage points (draw band -6.95 to 0.03) and -1.75 points (-3.31 to -0.19). Past and future histories did not differ clearly. Other higher areas had mean advantages of 4.55 and 1.55 points, but both bands included zero. Secondary spectral slopes were too uncertain to locate compression. Bands are mean plus or minus 1.96 SD over 12 overlapping draws, not independent confidence intervals. The original 32-mouse plan was reduced before neural score inspection because range reads were slow. This is a limited cross-clip test, not a full-cohort replication. Limits include two clips from one film, untested visual overlap, finite noisy source populations and higher capacity in lag models. Code, aggregate scores, full population spectra, provenance and regeneration instructions are included; external data remain outside the baseline bundle.

display.caption: Transfer scores and secondary spectral hierarchy slopes in eight mouse recordings. Each point averages 12 overlapping four-mouse target draws; bars show 1.96 SD, not independent confidence intervals. Predictor populations have 100 units and each target has 25. Models fit one named movie clip and predict the other. Spectral fits use ranks 2-10 and do not determine the location of compression.
